title: Omo Tuo
author: Akosua Mensah
desc: Two cups of jasmine rice to three of water, cooked until extremely soft and mashed hot — mushy, the source insists, but not mashed.
longDesc: Omo tuo is the Sunday accompaniment to groundnut and palm nut soup across Akan Ghana, and it is rice cooked deliberately past the point anyone would want to eat it loose. Two cups of jasmine rice, washed until the water runs clear, go into three cups of water and cook covered on medium-low until extremely soft and tender. While it is still hot, portions are gently mashed and shaped between wet hands. The source's own warning is the whole technique: it should not look like mashed potatoes, it should look mushy but not mashed.
ingredients: 2 cups jasmine rice, washed until the water runs clear
equipment: Bowl of water, for wetting the hands
steps: Wash the rice until the water runs clear.
Bring the rice and water to the boil over medium-high heat with salt to taste.
Reduce the heat to medium-low, cover, and cook until the rice is extremely soft and tender.
While it is still hot, gently mash portions of the rice.
Wet your hands and shape into balls.
Serve in a bowl with soup poured around them.
chefTips: The texture rule, and it is the only one that matters: it should not look like mashed potatoes, it should look mushy but not mashed. Some grain structure survives.
Mash it hot. Cooled rice will not come together and the balls fall apart in the soup.
Extremely soft and tender is the cue, which means cooking well past normal rice doneness. Properly cooked rice makes bad omo tuo.
Wash until the water runs clear. The loose starch would make it gluey rather than mushy.
Wet hands between every ball. Rice sticks harder than fufu does.
Three documented versions disagree sharply on water — 1.5, 1.75 and about 2.33 cups per cup of rice. This is the driest of the three; if your rice is not collapsing, the next one up is GHA004.
Gently is the operative word in the source's mashing instruction. Beating it develops the starch and gives you paste.
commonMistakes: Cooking the rice to normal doneness.
Mashing it once it has cooled.
Mashing hard enough to make a smooth paste.
sources: Adapted from 'Easy Omo Tuo Recipe — Ghanaian Rice Balls', savorythoughts.com. BYLINE FLAG: the byline prints as 'Savory Thoughts', the site's own name, not a person. Page metadata as printed: 6 Servings; prep 10, cook 20, total 30 minutes.
Quantities exactly as printed, and TWO-PASS consistent (the page was fetched twice and the figures matched): '2 Cups Jasmine Rice; Washed until the water runs clear'; '3 Cups Water'; 'Salt to taste'.

Method as printed, TWO-PASS: boil medium-high; 'reduce the heat to medium low, cover, and allow the rice to cook until extremely soft and tender'; 'gently mash portions of the rice while it's still hot'; wet the hands and shape.
THE TEXTURE NOTE, verbatim, and the most useful line on the page: 'It should not look like mashed potatoes. Rather, it should look mushy but not "mashed."'

THE WATER DISAGREEMENT ACROSS THREE DOCUMENTED VERSIONS, recorded unreconciled and not averaged. Water per cup of rice: 1.5 cups here; about 2.33 cups from Rachel @tastycurls via Le Creuset UK (GHA004); 1.75 cups from Nanasei Agyemang in Table Magazine New Mexico (GHA005). Cook times: 20 minutes here, 20-25 minutes (GHA004), 15-20 minutes (GHA005). Jasmine rice is specified in two of the three; the Le Creuset page says only 'rice' with no type.

A SOURCING NOTE WORTH STATING: no Ghanaian-authored omo tuo source was found. All three published versions are by non-Ghanaian authors or carry site-name bylines, which for a dish this central is a real gap in the record rather than a coincidence.
NOT USED: a Wikibooks 'Cookbook:Omo tuo' page was found and rejected for having no named author.
storage: 2 days refrigerated, wrapped so they do not dry out.
reheating: Steam briefly, or drop straight into hot soup.
healthBenefits: Easy to digest, which is why it is often given to the very young and the unwell.
Lower in calories per serving than fufu or banku.
culturalNote: Omo tuo is Sunday food in much of Ghana — the thing made after church to go with a long-cooked groundnut or palm nut soup, shaped into balls and set in the bowl for the soup to be poured over. The balls are eaten by pinching off pieces with the fingers of the right hand, the same way as fufu.
